title: Justice for a Coptic boy
hookLine: a well-known report tells how Umar punished a governor's son for striking an Egyptian: since when have you enslaved people born free

lines: I AM THE SON OF THE NOBLE ONES.
cards: A horse race in Egypt. Two young men, two horses, and the wrong one wins. The winner is a Copt, an Egyptian Christian.
The loser is the son of the governor, Amr ibn al-As, the man who rules the province for Umar. And the governor's son does what a certain kind of powerful young man does when he loses.
He takes a whip to the winner, and as he strikes he says: take that, I am the son of the noble ones. Today: justice for a Coptic boy.

teach.b: The story comes from a history of the conquest of Egypt, not from the hadith collections: a report people tell, not a verified hadith.
The Copt doesn't take the beating quietly. He travels all the way to Medina and stands before Umar. Umar listens, and sends for the governor and his son to come too.
When they arrive, Umar hands the whip to the Egyptian. Strike, he says, the son of the noble ones. And the Copt does.

Then Umar turns to the governor himself, the father whose name had made his son feel untouchable, and says the line the story is remembered for: since when have you enslaved people, when their mothers bore them free?
Not free because of your father's rank, or your tribe, or your faith. Free because you were born. And notice who stands where.
A Christian subject of a Muslim state crosses a desert to accuse the son of a Muslim governor, and the caliph hands him the whip.

teach.h: WHEN THEIR MOTHERS BORE THEM FREE.
teach.b: The Qur'an calls for this kind of evenhandedness: it tells believers to stand firm for justice as witnesses for God, even against themselves, or their parents, or their kin, whether rich or poor.
The story puts that verse on a dusty road between Egypt and Medina. Whatever happened on that road, the line is why the story lasts.

how: Muslims often quote Umar's line 'since when have you enslaved people when their mothers bore them free?' in sermons and writing on justice and human dignity, though the report comes from history, not the hadith collections.

games.why: the report says Umar summoned them both, handed the Copt the whip, then asked the father: since when have you enslaved people born free?

practice: Bring to mind someone who gets treated as smaller than they are: someone who cleans your office, a new kid at school, a neighbor whose accent people mock.
Say to yourself, about them, born free, and picture one quiet way to honor that, like using their name or thanking them in front of others.

wordCard.voice: Copt, an Egyptian Christian: the young man a governor's son struck with a whip, until Umar handed him the whip himself and asked, since when have you enslaved people born free? Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'free', the last word of Umar's line, people whose mothers bore them free.

carryVoice: Your line: born free. Not by rank, tribe or faith, but by birth. Day eight hundred seventy-four.
